title: Meta Finally Ditched the Cameras—and Made Its Best Smart Glasses Yet
gist: WIRED rates Meta's camera-free Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses ($349) 8/10. It argues that dropping the camera, after privacy backlash over "pervert glasses" and a facial-recognition lawsuit, makes them Meta's best smart glasses yet: lighter (43-47 g against 51.5 g), with 12-hour battery life and strong audio, though Meta AI is still not top-notch.

insights.claim: Meta's Ray-Ban Meta Audio smart glasses, announced in September, drop the camera entirely; the camera is the only big change from Meta's other glasses, and the reviewer says removing it makes the product better.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: A camera-free SKU widens Meta's wearables addressable market to buyers put off by recording hardware.
insights.quote: The only big change between these and Meta’s other glasses is the lack of a camera, but losing that one feature makes a world of difference.
insights.locator: This feature has long been available

insights.claim: The Ray-Ban Meta Audio glasses sell for $349 at both Ray-Ban and Meta and received an 8/10 rating from WIRED, with price and chunky frames listed as the main drawbacks.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: The $349 price point anchors audio-only smart-glasses pricing against earbuds and headphones.
insights.quote: Still pretty pricey. Chunkier than regular glasses.

insights.claim: The Ray-Ban Meta Audio frames weigh 43 grams (Burbank) and 47 grams (Clubmaster), lighter than the 51.5-gram camera-equipped Gen 3 Wayfarer, and offer a 12-hour battery life that makes all-day wear viable.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Dropping the camera buys weight and battery gains, the two main barriers to all-day wearables adoption.
insights.quote: A 12-hour battery life means all-day wear is truly viable.
insights.locator: They’re lightweight—43 grams for the Burbank

insights.claim: Meta's camera-equipped glasses drew waves of privacy controversy: critics called them "pervert glasses" after pickup artists used them to record people without consent, and users shared ways to remove the recording indicator light, which Meta countered with a software fix that disables the cameras if the light is tampered with.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Privacy backlash is a real adoption headwind and regulatory risk for camera-based wearables.
insights.quote: It took waves of privacy controversies for Meta to finally ditch the cameras.
insights.locator: It took waves of privacy controversies

insights.claim: Meta tried to put facial recognition on its glasses, first denied it, later admitted and removed it, and was sued in September over its facial recognition systems; Meta says the public pushback did not influence the audio-only release.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Pending facial-recognition litigation is a legal overhang on Meta's wearables line.
insights.quote: In September, the company was sued for its facial recognition systems.
insights.locator: It didn’t help that the company

insights.claim: Meta's camera-first approach to glasses reflects its core business: Facebook is a visual platform designed to capture content and beam it to the world.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Meta's hardware roadmap is shaped by its content-capture ad business, not only by what users want from wearables.
insights.quote: It makes sense that Meta started with cameras on its glasses.

insights.claim: The Meta Audio glasses do not record audio except during AI chatbot requests, which are saved in the Meta AI app; live language translation is available but requires opening the Meta AI app first.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Data capture still flows to Meta AI through voice queries, which keeps the AI engagement funnel going without cameras.
insights.quote: Those requests are then saved in the Meta AI app.
insights.locator: All that goes away when cameras

themes.theme: Audio-first use case and Meta AI quality

insights.claim: The reviewer used the glasses' Meta AI voice assistant for turn-by-turn directions while running in Los Angeles; the navigation was imperfect but got him back.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Voice-agent navigation is a working but unpolished use case, showing where AI assistant quality still trails.
insights.quote: The navigation wasn’t perfect, but it got me where I needed to be.
insights.locator: The music dims, and the AI

insights.claim: The Ray-Ban Meta Audio pairs fast-adjusting transition lenses with speakers that mix music and ambient sound and have good call quality, though sound leaks out and bass is weak, which the reviewer says makes them possibly the perfect running glasses.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Fitness and running are a clear wedge for audio glasses that replace earbuds.
insights.quote: the Ray-Ban Meta Audio might just be the perfect running glasses
insights.locator: The frames may be thick, but

insights.claim: WIRED rates Meta AI on the glasses as improving but not top-notch.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Assistant quality is the main software gap for Meta wearables against rivals.
insights.quote: Meta AI is getting better, but isn’t top-notch.

insights.claim: Having tried many smart glasses this year, most of which end up in a drawer, the reviewer says the Ray-Ban Meta Audio are probably the only ones he would buy with his own money; he hints that Google might eventually beat Meta.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Meta leads on everyday wearability for now, but Google is flagged as the likely challenger to watch.
insights.quote: Maybe somebody (cough Google cough) will beat Meta eventually.
insights.locator: Frankly, these are probably the only

insights.claim: Cameras remain necessary for augmented-reality smart glasses, but the reviewer argues removing them is the right choice for anyone who isn't using smart glasses to capture content, which points to a split between AR/capture devices and audio-first devices.
insights.speaker: Boone Ashworth
insights.so_what: Expect the category to split into camera/AR and audio-only tiers with different price and privacy profiles.
insights.quote: Anything with augmented reality features will need them.
insights.locator: I also like that I can walk
